findings.evidence: Table 4-2, TTFT budget row: "TTFT budget | 1.2 s (retrieval ~120 ms + prefill ~1.08 s); p95 ceiling ≤ 2 s | [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]". The row-level label is [ASSUMPTION]. However, Table 4-1's Latency row derivation note (p.62) explicitly states: "the 1.2 s TTFT and ~25 ms TPOT targets are the [ASSUMPTION]; the ~1.08 s prefill figure inside the TTFT budget is [canonical scenario][DERIVED] = TTFT − retrieval". The TTFT budget of 1.2 s is an author-chosen target in Table 4-1 but is labeled [ASSUMPTION] in Table 4-2's TTFT budget row (which is the row-level label for the entire TTFT entry). This is consistent — but check also: the 'prefill compute budget' row (p.77) says "Prefill compute budget — two-term-only upper cap, NOT a feasible deployed prefill target | 1.08 s | [canonical scenario][DERIVED] = TTFT budget (1.2 s) − retrieval (120 ms)" — correctly derived from two assumptions. The problem is the TTFT budget row itself: it labels the 1.2 s as [ASSUMPTION] when the derivation of the whole row (1.2 s = retrieval + prefill budget) treats the components as separated into one assumed (1.2 s target) and one derived (1.08 s prefill). The row's [ASSUMPTION] label is for the 1.2 s target — correct. BUT the row shows a composite value (1.2 s with its internal decomposition) and assigns one label to both components. The 1.2 s is [ASSUMPTION], the 1.08 s is [DERIVED]; the row gives only [ASSUMPTION], omitting the derived component's status. This conflates two label axes in one cell.
findings.issue: Table 4-2's TTFT budget row assigns a single [ASSUMPTION] label to a composite value whose two components have different epistemic statuses: the 1.2 s target is [ASSUMPTION] but the ~1.08 s prefill residual is [DERIVED] (= 1.2 − 0.12). The 'prefill compute budget' row separately labels 1.08 s as [DERIVED], showing the book knows the distinction, but the TTFT budget row's cell shows both values under one label, hiding that the decomposition contains a derived quantity.
findings.fix_instruction: In Table 4-2's TTFT budget row (p.76), either split the value cell into separate rows for the 1.2 s assumption and the 1.08 s derived residual (each with its own label), or add an inline note: 'the 1.2 s target is [ASSUMPTION]; the 1.08 s prefill residual = 1.2 − 0.12 is [DERIVED]' — matching how Table 4-1's latency row explicitly makes this split.

findings.evidence: Table 4-2, Mean request service time row (p.66): "Mean request service time (planning headline — not used for occupancy) | ~10 s [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] — an author-chosen round planning headline. The budget-derived components are retrieval ~120 ms + prefill budget cap ~1.08 s + decode ~7.5 s = ~8.7 s, plus ~15% planning headroom to ~10 s."
findings.issue: The row is labeled [ASSUMPTION] alone, but the derivation note states an explicit arithmetic: ~8.7 s components + ~15% headroom → ~10 s. Under the book's own convention (Table 4-2 Note 1, p.77: 'a value arithmetically derived from those assumed inputs … is [canonical scenario][DERIVED]'), the ~10 s is computed from stated components and should carry [ASSUMPTION][DERIVED] or at minimum a note that the [ASSUMPTION] label covers only the ~15% headroom input, not the arithmetic that produces the final figure. The current single [ASSUMPTION] label on a computed value contradicts the labeling rule the same table's Note 1 defines.
findings.fix_instruction: Change the label on the Mean request service time row from '[canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]' to '[canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION][DERIVED]' — or restructure the derivation to show the [ASSUMPTION] applies to the headroom input and [DERIVED] to the ~10 s total — consistent with Note 1's rule on page 77.

findings.evidence: Table 4-2 Note 1 (p.77): "a vendor hardware constant (e.g. the H100 footprint) is [1P][FACT], never [ILLUSTRATIVE]; … [canonical scenario] is distinct from [ILLUSTRATIVE], which is reserved for a non-canonical hypothetical and uses the same ASSUMPTION/DERIVED split." Meanwhile, Ch. 3 Table 3-1 (p.41) labels the canonical dense 70B geometry as '[canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]' and Ch. 1's KV formula derivation (p.7) cites the 7B-class geometry as '32 layers, d_hidden 4096' without any label. The 70B reference geometry (80 layers, hidden 8192) is not a vendor hardware constant — it is a constructed teaching geometry [ASSUMPTION] — but the 8×H100 host (640 GB pool) mixes [1P][FACT] per-GPU constants (80 GB) with [ASSUMPTION] deployment-unit choices. Note 1 does not explicitly address a cell that contains both a [1P][FACT] component and a [ASSUMPTION] component (e.g. the Hardware row: '8×H100 (80 GB each, 640 GB)' with no label on the row itself in the Canonical Workload box, while Table 4-2's per-GPU rows are [1P][FACT]).
findings.issue: Table 4-2's Note 1 defines rules for single provenance types but does not address composite values that blend [1P][FACT] components (the 80 GB per-GPU capacity) with [ASSUMPTION] components (the 8-GPU deployment choice, the 640 GB aggregate). The Hardware row in the Canonical Workload box (p.68) shows '8×H100 (80 GB each, 640 GB)' with no label at all, leaving the reader unable to tell whether 80 GB is a vendor fact and 8 GPUs is a scenario choice, or vice versa.
findings.fix_instruction: Add an inline label to the Hardware row in the Canonical Workload box: '8×H100 (80 GB each [1P][FACT], 8-GPU count [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION], 640 GB aggregate [1P][FACT] × 8)'. Also add a sentence to Table 4-2's Note 1 defining how to label a value whose components span different provenance types.

findings.evidence: Active-hours volume is ~6.24M requests/month (10 × 3,600 × 8 × 260/12 = 6,240,000). Over 24×7 the same 10 rps would extrapolate to ~18.7M requests/month on the same 260-workday calendar (10 × 3,600 × 24 × 260/12 = 18,720,000)
findings.issue: The 24×7 extrapolation formula is arithmetically wrong as written: 10 × 3,600 × 24 × 260/12 = 187,200,000, not 18,720,000. The stated result 18.7M is off by a factor of 10. Check: 10 × 3,600 = 36,000 s/hr-worth of requests; × 24 hr = 864,000; × 260 workdays = 224,640,000; ÷ 12 months = 18,720,000 per month when multiplied by 260/12 — but that is 18,720,000 only if the 260/12 factor is applied to a month count of 260 days giving 21.67 days per month... The correct arithmetic for a 260-workday year spread over 12 months is 36,000 × 24 × 260/12 = 18,720,000 per month, i.e. the factor 260/12 must multiply 36,000 × 24 × 12/12; as printed the expression evaluates to 187.2M. The reader cannot reproduce the stated 18.7M from the printed formula, and the '3× the active-hours volume' claim (6.24M × 3 = 18.72M) is consistent only with the intended value, not the printed expression.
findings.fix_instruction: Correct the formula to 10 × 3,600 × 24 × 260 ÷ 12 = 18,720,000 (or equivalently 36,000 × 24 × 21.67 days/month ≈ 18.72M), and state the days-per-month step explicitly so the expression evaluates to the printed result.

findings.evidence: Average arrival rate ~10 rps [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] declared traffic input (2,000 users × one request ~every 200 s ≈ 10 rps) — declared, not derived (walk-through below).
findings.issue: The declared traffic input is arithmetically inconsistent with its own stated derivation: 2,000 users × one request every 200 s = 2,000/200 = 10 requests/s only if every registered user issues a request every 200 s continuously. The derivation is fine in isolation, but the chapter elsewhere (Preface p. xiv, Ch. 4 §4.8) treats the same 2,000-user population as 5% active (~100 users), which would imply 100/200 = 0.5 rps, not 10 rps — a 20× discrepancy between the population model and the declared rate. The chapter's own walk-through §4.3 step 3 insists the rate is 'declared, not derived', but the printed parenthetical supplies a derivation that conflicts with the stated 5% active fraction. A reader re-deriving the rate from either population figure cannot land on 10 rps.
findings.fix_instruction: Either make the parenthetical derivation self-consistent (state which sub-population of the 2,000 registered users issues one request per 200 s — e.g. 2,000 registered users including automation/API callers, or ~2,000 concurrent-capable seats — and remove the implication that this equals the 5% active-user population), or explicitly annotate that the 200 s interval applies to the full registered population while the 5% figure is a concurrent-activity measure, and note that the two are not the same denominator.

findings.evidence: Execution occupancy ~86 requests at 10 rps; ~344 at 40 rps — [canonical scenario][DERIVED] via Little's Law Lexec = λ × Wexec ... service time Wexec ≈ 8.6 s
findings.issue: The canonical box states Wexec ≈ 8.6 s (prefill 1.08 s + decode 7.5 s = 8.58 s). Little's Law with λ=10 and W=8.58 gives 85.8 → ~86 ✓ and λ=40 gives 343.2 → ~344 ✓, so the occupancy figures are arithmetically sound. However the box prints the prefill term as 1.08 s, which Table 4-2 and Ch. 2 explicitly label a 'two-term-only upper cap, NOT a feasible deployed prefill target' (budget_prefill ≤ 1.08 s − B_other). Using the upper cap as the Wexec input makes the occupancy figures and every downstream host count (⌈344/17⌉ = 21, Ch. 17) inherit the cap rather than a modelled runtime, but neither the box nor Ch. 16–17 states this inheritance explicitly; Ch. 4 §4.3 does add 'So Wexec ≈ 8.6 s is an upper bound on the execution window'. The defect is a labelling gap: the '~86' and '~344' rows carry [canonical scenario][DERIVED] with no marker that the input is a budget cap and therefore an upper bound on occupancy (and thus on host count), which understates the fleet requirement.
findings.fix_instruction: Mark the Execution occupancy row's status as an upper-bound derivation (e.g. [canonical scenario][DERIVED] — upper bound, Wexec input is the 1.08 s prefill cap; occupancy falls if B_other is measured) and add the same caveat to the host-count figures that consume 86/344 in Ch. 17 Table 17-1.

findings.evidence: nhosts = ⌈50 rps × 8.6 s / 17 slots⌉ = ⌈430/17⌉ = ⌈25.29⌉ = 26 hosts (full utilization) and on the u-only screen at a 70% target utilization the normative host-count form of Ch 17 Table 17-1 gives ⌈26 ÷ 0.70⌉ = ⌈37.14⌉ = 38 hosts
findings.issue: Internal inconsistency in the u-only cross-check. The chapter states '⌈26 ÷ 0.70⌉ = ⌈37.14⌉ = 38 hosts' but 26 ÷ 0.70 = 37.14 and ⌈37.14⌉ = 38 ✓; however it then states 'the occupancy cross-check ⌈430/(17 × 0.7)⌉ = ⌈430/11.9⌉ = ⌈36.13⌉ = 37 sits one host below it'. The two forms are then declared to 'reproduce the normative result at the policy stage (40 provisioned / 39 working)' — but the cross-check form at the policy stage is given as ⌈430/(17 × 0.70 × 0.95)⌉ = ⌈430/11.305⌉ = ⌈38.04⌉ = 39, and the host-count form ⌈26 ÷ 0.665⌉ = ⌈39.10⌉ = 40. The narrative therefore reports two different 'reproduces the normative result' claims (one at 38 vs 37 and one at 39 vs 40) and each time the two forms differ by one host — the text says the cross-check 'reproduces the normative result' while simultaneously showing it does not. The rule that the cross-check 'may differ by one host' is correct, but the claim that it 'reproduces the normative result' at the policy stage is false for the stated numbers (39 ≠ 40).
findings.fix_instruction: Correct the sentence: state that the occupancy cross-check differs from the normative host-count form by one host at every stage (38 vs 37 at u-only; 40 vs 39 at policy), and that the normative form is the one quoted (40 provisioned / 39 working), with the cross-check reported as a bound rather than as reproducing the result.

findings.evidence: Cost-basis reconciliation ... (c) ~$0.0033 per request (≈$3.33 per 1K) — owned fleet, 6-host average at full utilization on the hour-matched active-hours basis ($120/hr × 173.33 h ≈ $20,800/mo ÷ 6.24M requests); (d) ~$0.0140 per request (≈$14.04 per 1K) — the same owned 6-host fleet paid for all 730 h/mo and divided by the same active-hours volume
findings.issue: The (c)/(d) reconciliation is arithmetically correct ($20,800/6.24M = $0.00333; $87,600/6.24M = $0.01404; ratio 4.21 = 730/173.33 ✓) but the derived figures contradict the per-request owned-fleet figure quoted earlier in the same chapter on p. 84: '(6 × $20/hr) ÷ (10 × 3600) ≈ ~$0.0033 per request at average'. The $0.0033 figure there is obtained by dividing hourly spend by hourly request rate (a pure rate ratio), which equals the hour-matched monthly figure only by coincidence of the 173.33/10 arithmetic — and the chapter's own hour-basis-mismatch argument applies to it: $120/hr ÷ 10 rps = $0.0033/req is a rate-basis figure that happens to match the active-hours monthly figure because both use the same hour count, but the p. 84 text presents the 6/21-host 'full-util basis' as a third and fourth number ($0.0056 / $0.0044 on the policy fleet) without noting these are also hour-basis artifacts. The result is five or more per-request owned-fleet figures across §4.3 with no single canonical statement of which one is quotable, and the canonical-box sidebar (p. 72) explicitly says 'None of those three is an alternative unit cost' while §4.3 quotes them side by side as if they were.
findings.fix_instruction: Add a single named canonical per-request owned-fleet figure with its basis (e.g. 'owned fleet, hour-matched active-hours basis, 6-host average: ~$0.0033/req') and mark every other per-request figure ($0.0140, $0.0056, $0.0044) explicitly as an hour-basis artifact or policy-fleet variant in a single consolidated table, rather than restating them across §4.3's prose, the cost-basis table and the sidebar.

findings.evidence: a canonical-box availability-topology note ... The canonical cost figures (Ch 16 $/1K req, Ch 17 host counts) therefore understate the cost of the canonical workload's own stated 99.9% availability requirement. Treat the TCO/fleet totals as single-region, N−1-only numbers, and add a separate multi-region capacity + replication cost line before the availability SLA can be considered met. The only multi-region price anywhere in the chapter is the illustrative ~2× infrastructure multiplier in §4.6, and it carries the same UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED status inline
findings.issue: The chapter states the ~2× multi-region multiplier is the 'only multi-region price anywhere in the chapter' and is UNPRICED / NOT VALIDATED, yet the Canonical Workload box itself (Table 4-1 Operational constraints row, p. 63) records the requirement as '[canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] author-chosen availability/operational requirement (99.9% SLA, multi-region active-active, daily embedding refresh)' and the Canonical Workload box's Availability row records '99.9%' as a canonical field with no UNPRICED marker — so the workload ledger presents the multi-region active-active topology as a settled canonical input while the cost arithmetic refuses to price it. The contradiction is that the canonical box is the book's single authoritative reference set ('When a chapter states a workload parameter, it comes from here and nowhere else'), so a downstream reader who pulls '99.9% availability, multi-region active-active' from the ledger and a '$3.33/1K' fleet cost from Ch. 16 is combining an unpriced topology with a single-region price without the ledger saying so.
findings.fix_instruction: In the Canonical Workload box and Table 4-1's Operational constraints row, tag the multi-region active-active topology explicitly as 'UNPRICED — no cost line exists in this edition (see availability-topology note)' so the ledger cannot be read as pricing a multi-region deployment, and add a one-line pointer in the Availability row to the same note.

findings.evidence: Preface: "The deployment unit those constants are priced into — an 8×H100 host — is a scenario choice, not a vendor fact: [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION], as Table 4-2 records it." Table 4-2's only host-related row is "Host price (8×H100, on-demand) ~$20/hr [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] dated price snapshot (2026 on-demand $2.50/GPU-hr × 8; not [1P] vendor spec, not a measured figure)" — its tag covers the price snapshot; no row states the host unit itself as [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] (the 80 GB-per-GPU and 640 GB pool constants are separately tagged [1P][FACT] in Table 7-1).
findings.issue: Cross-reference/support mismatch: the Preface attributes the 8×H100-host [ASSUMPTION] tagging to Table 4-2, but Table 4-2 contains no host-composition row carrying that tag — only the price row, whose Assumption status attaches to the $/hr snapshot, not to the 8-GPU deployment unit.
findings.fix_instruction: Add an explicit "Deployment unit — 8×H100 host" row to Table 4-2 tagged [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] (with the H100 per-GPU constants cross-referenced as [1P][FACT]), or reword the Preface to "as the Canonical Workload box records it".
